name: LM3880MF-1AA_NOPB
title: LM3880 three-rail power supply sequencer, 6-pin SOT-23
summary: A sequencer that releases three open-drain flags one after another when its EN input goes high, and pulls them low again in a set order when EN falls, so three regulators can be started and stopped in turn. Six internal timers, fixed in EEPROM at the factory, set the delays; the order codes pick one of six delay sets (2 ms to 120 ms) and the sequence number picks the power-down order. It runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, draws 25 µA typical, and up to three can be chained for nine rails. LM3880MF-1AA/NOPB is sequence 1 (up 1-2-3, down 3-2-1) with 10 ms on every timer, 1000 parts on a small reel.
key_figures: three open-drain flags, VOL 0.4 V max at 1.2 mA

notes: Order code: LM3880 (LM3880Q for the automotive grade), then MFE, MF or MFX for 250, 1000 or 3000 parts per reel, then the sequence number, then the timing designator. All parts in the catalogue are sequence 1.
Sequence 1 raises the flags 1-2-3 and lowers them 3-2-1. Other sequences and delays are factory options on request.
The .B variants have RoHS "-", lead finish and MSL "Call TI", and no marking.
An automotive version, LM3880-Q1, qualified to AEC-Q100, exists.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable with a precise 1.25 V threshold and an internal 7 µA pull-up. Rising starts the power-up sequence; falling starts the power-down sequence.

pins.name: FLAG3
pins.function: Open-drain flag 3, released last on power-up in sequence 1.

pins.name: FLAG1
pins.function: Open-drain flag 1, released first on power-up.

circuits.title: Typical application: three supplies in sequence
circuits.description: U1 runs from the input supply and takes its start command on EN. Each flag has a 100 kΩ pull-up to the input supply, and each flag line goes to the enable input of one regulator. With sequence 1 and 30 ms timing, the rails come up 1, 2, 3 and go down 3, 2, 1.

circuits.title: Sequencing with a separate flag supply
circuits.description: The same sequencer with its three pull-ups tied to a separate flag supply instead of VCC, so the flag high level suits enable inputs that need another voltage. The flag supply must stay at or below VCC + 0.3 V.

circuits.title: EN delayed by a capacitor (power-up sequencing only)
circuits.description: A capacitor from EN to ground is charged by the 7 µA internal pull-up, so the sequence starts a set time after VCC comes up. The flags fall together with the supply on power-down rather than in sequence.

parts.note: sets the start delay, tenable_delay = 1.25 V × CEN / 7 µA

circuits.title: EN from a divider on the input supply (power-up sequencing only)
circuits.description: R4 and R5 divide the input supply onto EN, so the sequence starts once the supply passes a chosen level. The divider values must allow for the internal 7 µA EN pull-up current. Power-down is not sequenced.

circuits.title: EN from an external signal (power-up and power-down sequencing)
circuits.description: EN is driven by an outside logic signal, such as a microcontroller GPIO, so both the rise and the fall of the rails are sequenced.

where.tenable_delay: time from VCC rising until EN reaches its threshold

operation.text: At power-up all three flags are held low until EN goes above its threshold. Then timer 1 runs and FLAG1 is released at its end; timer 2 then starts and releases FLAG2, and timer 3 releases FLAG3.

When EN falls, timers 4, 5 and 6 pull the flags low one after another, in the reverse order for sequence 1 (FLAG3, then FLAG2, then FLAG1). The three power-down timers are set apart from the power-up ones.

All six delays come from one master clock with a very low temperature coefficient, so they track each other and hold over temperature. Timers 1 and 4 run about 400 µs longer than programmed, the time of an EPROM refresh; this matters only for the shortest delays.

EN feeds a comparator set by a 1.25 V bandgap reference, with a 7 µA internal pull-up. It can be driven by logic, held off by a capacitor for a delay from VCC, or fed by a resistor divider to start at a supply level; divider values must allow for the pull-up current.
Timer 1 starts counting at the rising threshold but restarts from zero if EN drops before FLAG1 is released, so a short EN pulse releases nothing.

If EN falls after FLAG1 is out but before the power-up run is complete, the running timer resets, the remaining flags are still released, and the power-down sequence begins about 120 ms after the last flag.

If EN rises after the first timer has finished but before power-down is complete, the running timer resets, the power-down run is completed, and power-up starts about 120 ms after the last flag falls.
Each open-drain flag needs a pull-up; 100 kΩ is the value given. The pull-up rail may be VCC or a separate supply no higher than VCC + 0.3 V.

EN should not be tied straight to VCC: the flags may misbehave, most of all when VCC rises slowly. Keep EN below threshold until VCC is above 2.7 V. A capacitor or divider on EN sequences power-up only; the flags then drop with the supply. For sequenced power-down too, drive EN from a separate signal.
Up to three LM3880 can be chained to sequence nine rails.
VCC should sit close to its source. No input capacitor is required; where VCC is noisy, a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass may be added.
Put the flag pull-ups near the part and near the flag supply with short traces. Where flag timing must be tight, route the flag lines short and of equal length to the inputs they drive.
